entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ allowing for the traffic was heavy → allowing for traffic, or allowing for the fact that traffic was heavy). The for is part of the word: dropping it gives you the plain verb, and allowing the traffic means something else entirely.
entries.pattern: Allowing for [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] allowing for [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Three words adjust a figure and they are not interchangeable. Allowing for X builds X into the estimate and keeps it in view; excluding X takes X out of the arithmetic; discounting X dismisses X as not worth counting. Barring is different again — it names a future spoiler rather than a known factor. Against given, which accepts a premise whole, allowing for concedes only a partial adjustment.
entries.meaning: Makes room in a claim for a factor the speaker already knows about. It is the honest hedge of estimates, budgets, and forecasts. 1. Adjusting a figure for a known factor. The quantitative use. 2. Making allowance for a person's circumstances. The excusing use, close to considering.
examples: Allowing for inflation, the raise is closer to two percent.
Allowing for traffic, the drive takes an hour and a half.
Allowing for rounding, the two totals match.
The schedule holds, allowing for one weather day.
Even allowing for his inexperience, the mistake was serious.
Allowing for being new to the system, she has picked it up fast.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ barring that the weather holds). Pronoun objects take the objective case: barring him.
entries.pattern: Barring [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] barring [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Barring is hypothetical and forward-looking — it names the one thing that could still spoil a prediction. Excepting and excluding subtract something that actually exists. The bare form bar (bar a miracle) is chiefly British; American English keeps bar only in the fixed phrase bar none.
variants: bar (British; in American English only in bar none)
entries.meaning: Frozen from the verb bar, "to block." It sets one obstacle in front of an otherwise confident claim and is overwhelmingly a sentence-opener. 1. Unless this one thing intervenes. The default use, always about the future. 2. With the exception of. A weaker, static use, close to apart from.
examples: Barring a last-minute appeal, the sale closes Friday.
Barring bad weather, we should be in Denver by six.
The team makes the playoffs barring another injury at quarterback.
Barring a few typos, the manuscript is clean.
Barring the second chapter, I liked the book.
She has the votes, barring something nobody has thought of yet.
Barring being called in to cover a shift, I'm free all weekend.

entries.register: archaic; alive only in legal and antiquarian prose
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause in modern use. Do not write bating that.
entries.pattern: bating [noun phrase] · Bating [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: A dead synonym of excepting and barring. Clipped from abating, from the verb abate, "to subtract." Do not confuse it with baiting (luring) or with bated in with bated breath, which is the same root in a different sense — "restrained."
entries.meaning: Subtracts an item from a total or a claim. Any modern sentence that uses it is either quoting an old document or making a joke about one; except for is the living equivalent.
examples: Bating a few errors of arithmetic, the accounts were in order.
The whole estate passed to the widow, bating the mill.
Bating his temper, he was an excellent tenant.
Every witness agreed, bating the clerk.
She was, bating one bad season, the best pitcher in the league.

entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard word in notices and official announcements
entries.complement: a time expression only — a date, a day, or a prepositional phrase of time (beginning in July, beginning at noon). Never a finite clause, and never an ordinary object (✗ beginning the project in this sense, which is the plain verb).
entries.pattern: Beginning [date], [main clause]. · [main clause] beginning [date].
entries.contrast: Starting is the everyday equivalent and is what Americans say out loud; beginning is the version that gets printed on the sign. As of can look backward as well as forward (as of Tuesday, we had no answer); beginning only looks forward. From needs a matching endpoint or an on to feel complete.
entries.meaning: A pure scheduling word. It fixes the first day of a new arrangement and says nothing about when the arrangement ends.
examples: Beginning Monday, the clinic opens at seven.
Rates increase beginning January 1.
Beginning in the fall, all freshmen live on campus.
The library will close at six beginning next week.
Beginning with the third episode, the show finds its footing.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or wh-nominal (concerning what happened) — never a finite that-clause. To take a clause you need concerning the fact that, which is worse than starting over.
entries.pattern: concerning [noun phrase] · Concerning [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: Concerning, regarding, respecting, touching, and re all mean "about," but only the first two are still in ordinary use, and concerning is the heavier of those two — it belongs to correspondence and reports. In speech, plain about is almost always the better word. Note that the adjective concerning — "a concerning trend," meaning worrying — is a separate, much newer American usage and is not this word.
entries.meaning: The formal topic preposition: it names what a document, question, or complaint is about.
examples: I have a question concerning the deadline.
The memo says nothing concerning severance.
Concerning your invoice, we never received it.
She wrote to the board concerning the audit.
Rumors concerning the merger have been circulating for weeks.
There is a statute concerning exactly this situation.

entries.type: marginal/participial; also a subordinating conjunction with that, and an absolute adverb
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a finite clause with or without that — considering (that) she had never flown before. It is the one word in this file that freely takes a clause in ordinary American English. It can also stand alone with no complement at all: She did well, considering.
entries.pattern: Considering [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Considering (that) [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], considering.
entries.contrast: Against given: both accept a fact and reason from it, but given is clipped and treats the fact as a settled premise, while considering implies weighing and leans toward excusing what follows. Only considering can trail a sentence alone (✗ She did well, given). Do not confuse it with concerning — considering the evidence means in view of it, concerning the evidence means about it.
entries.meaning: The workhorse of the group, and the only one that has kept a foot in three word classes at once. 1. In view of; taking into account. With a noun phrase. 2. Seeing that. With a full clause, functioning as a conjunction. 3. All things considered. Standing alone at the end of a sentence, as an adverb.
examples: Considering her age, she recovered remarkably fast.
The price is fair considering the condition of the roof.
Considering the hour, the crowd was enormous.
Considering that he had two hours' notice, the speech was excellent.
Considering you've never done this before, that's impressive.
Considering having to learn the software from scratch, she was quick.
The turnout was good, considering.
It went well, considering — nobody walked out.

entries.register: informal to neutral; a spoken word
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (not counting waiting for a table) — never a finite clause (✗ not counting that the kids came). Almost always negated: not counting.
entries.pattern: counting [noun phrase] · not counting [noun phrase] · [main clause], not counting [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Counting is the conversational including, and it is restricted to tallies — you can say counting the dog about a headcount, but not counting Chapter 4 about a table of contents. Negative not counting is the spoken excluding.
entries.meaning: The arithmetic preposition of everyday speech. It adds or, more often, withholds an item from a running total. 1. Including in a total. Positive, usually about people or money. 2. Excluding from a total. The far more common negative, not counting.
examples: There are nine of us, counting the kids.
Counting tips, she clears about forty thousand.
It's a two-hour drive, not counting traffic.
We've lost three games, not counting the exhibition.
The room sleeps six, not counting the couch.
Counting the garage, the place is nineteen hundred square feet.
It's ninety minutes at that place, not counting waiting for a table.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a wh-nominal — and the wh-nominal is the everyday form: depending on what he says, depending on whether it rains, depending on how many show up. Never a bare that-clause (✗ depending on that it rains). ✗ Depending of and ✗ depending from are errors; the adjective is dependent on or dependent upon, never dependent of.
entries.pattern: Depending on [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause], depending on [noun phrase or wh-clause].
entries.contrast: Three near neighbors sort by what the object names. Depending on names the variable that will decide the outcome; based on names the evidence a conclusion rests on; according to names the source of a report. So the price varies depending on the season (variable), we chose based on the reviews (evidence), according to the reviews, it's good (source). Keep the preposition apart from the plain verb: the outcome depends on the vote is a verb with a subject, while depending on the vote, we may adjourn has no subject and is a preposition.
entries.meaning: Names the thing that has not been settled yet and that will settle everything else. It is the standard way American English hedges a quantity, a schedule, or a decision. 1. Determined by; varying with. With a noun phrase — the range use. 2. Conditional on the answer to a question. With a wh- or whether-nominal.
examples: Depending on the weather, the game starts at six or not at all.
Tickets run $40 to $90, depending on the seat.
Depending on what the lab says, we may operate tonight.
Depending on whether the bill passes, the rate changes in July.
She works from home two or three days, depending on the week.
Depending on how you count, there are eight planets or nine.

entries.register: neutral to formal; common in analysis and argument
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: Discounting [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] discounting [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Excluding removes an item as a matter of arithmetic; discounting dismisses it as not worth weighing. The difference is judgment: excluding the outliers is a method, discounting the outliers is an argument. Not counting is the casual version of excluding, never of this.
entries.meaning: Sets something aside on the grounds that it should not count — because it is unreliable, unrepresentative, or interested. It carries an implicit claim, which is why it belongs to persuasion rather than bookkeeping.
examples: Discounting the outliers, the results are consistent.
Discounting his own testimony, there is no evidence at all.
Sales rose eight percent, discounting the effect of the promotion.
Discounting inflation, wages have been flat for a decade.
Even discounting the hype, the device is impressive.
Discounting having played at home all month, the streak still means something.

entries.ipa: /ˈdʊrɪŋ/, widely /ˈdɜrɪŋ/ (rhyming with stirring) · casual /ˈdɜrɪn/ · British keeps the yod: /ˈdjʊərɪŋ/
entries.type: marginal/participial by origin, now a fully grammaticalized simple preposition
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period or an event — never a finite clause (✗ during I was there → while I was there), never a gerund (✗ during eating → while eating), and never a measure of duration (✗ during three hours → for three hours).
entries.pattern: during [noun phrase] · During [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: The big one is during vs. for: for answers "how long" and takes a quantity (for two weeks), while during answers "when" and takes a named span (during the strike). for · While is the clause form; throughout insists on the entire span, where during leaves the point inside it vague.
entries.meaning: Historically a participle — the object of the obsolete verb dure, "to last," in an absolute construction (during the king's life once meant "the king's life enduring"). Nothing of that survives in the modern word except its membership in this file. 1. At some point inside a period. The event is located somewhere within the span. 2. Throughout a period. The event occupies the whole span.
examples: She called during the meeting.
The power went out twice during the storm.
He worked two jobs during college.
During the strike, the plant produced nothing.
Nobody speaks during the reading.
During the sixties, the town lost half its population.

entries.register: formal and dated; standard only after not and always
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause in modern American English. The old conjunction excepting that is archaic.
entries.pattern: not excepting [noun phrase] · always excepting [noun phrase] · Excepting [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: Plain except is the ordinary word, and using excepting where except would do sounds stilted or legalistic. Between the two live forms, the rule is positional: at the front of a sentence American English requires except for (Except for the ending, the movie is great; ✗ Except the ending, the movie is great), while after the noun either works (everyone except him, everyone except for him). Excepting can front on its own, which is the one thing it still does that except cannot. Excepting otherwise survives in two fixed frames: not excepting (which insists someone is included) and always excepting (a legal reservation). The postposed participle excepted is alive and well.
entries.meaning: An older, heavier except. Note that not excepting means the opposite of what learners expect — it does not exclude anyone; it refuses to exclude them.
examples: Everyone signed, not excepting the chairman.
The rule applies to all staff, always excepting the medical team.
Excepting the last chapter, the book is a delight.
All fees are refundable, excepting the deposit.
Every state ratified it, not excepting the two that had sued.

entries.register: neutral; the default in commercial, technical, and statistical writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] excluding [noun phrase] · Excluding [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: The exact opposite of including, and the neutral partner of not counting. Against except for: excluding is arithmetical and unemotional, while except for often implies the exception is remarkable. Exclusive of is the formal contract-drafting version. Against discounting: excluding removes, discounting dismisses.
entries.meaning: Subtracts a specified item from a set, a total, or a price. It makes no claim about why.
examples: The fare is $340, excluding taxes and fees.
Excluding weekends, that leaves eleven working days.
Enrollment rose in every division, excluding the law school.
The study covered adults, excluding anyone over eighty.
Excluding the two pilot sites, results were flat.
The job takes four hours, excluding driving out and back.

entries.complement: noun phrase, typically abstract (an agreement, a payment, a response) or the pronoun that — never a finite clause (✗ failing that they agree → failing agreement).
entries.pattern: Failing [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Failing that, [main clause].
entries.contrast: Failing and barring are mirror images. Barring X means "unless X happens," where X is the obstacle; failing X means "if X does not happen," where X is the thing you were hoping for. Absent and in the absence of are the near-synonyms; failing that is the fixed phrase that carries the whole word in everyday writing.
entries.meaning: Introduces the fallback. It names the thing that was supposed to occur and quietly concedes that it might not. 1. If the named thing does not happen. With an abstract noun phrase, and always fronted. 2. Failing that. The fixed phrase, which carries the word in everyday writing and is the only form most Americans ever use.
examples: Failing an agreement by Friday, the case goes to trial.
Failing payment within thirty days, the account goes to collections.
Failing any response from the seller, the buyer may cancel.
Ask your supervisor; failing that, put it in writing to HR.
We'll take the early flight, or failing that, drive.
Try the main number, and failing that, email the clerk.

entries.register: neutral to formal; heavy in journalism and official statements
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause (✗ following she resigned → after she resigned, or following her resignation). A gerund is grammatical but nearly always clumsy (following being notified → following notification), so the repair for a tempting clause is a nominalization, not an -ing form. The demonstrative pronoun is fine: following that, we adjourned.
entries.pattern: Following [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] following [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: After is the plain word, it can take a clause, and it is almost always better. Following implies the second event came because of the first, which is exactly why press releases prefer it — and exactly why it should be resisted when no such link exists. Subsequent to is worse than either. Do not let it collide with the noun the following (please read the following).
entries.meaning: The journalist's after. It attaches an event to the trigger that preceded it, and it dangles easily: Following the vote, the room emptied is fine, but Following the vote, applause broke out invites the reading that the applause did the following. 1. After, in plain sequence. No causal claim — the second event simply came later. 2. In the wake of; as a result of. The loaded use, and the reason press offices reach for the word.
examples: Following a brief recess, the hearing resumed.
Following his release, he moved to Arizona.
Following the storm, half the county was without power.
Three executives resigned following the audit.
The bill was withdrawn following pressure from both parties.
Following that, we adjourned until Thursday.

entries.complement: a number or a number-headed time or age expression — never a clause, never a person or an object (✗ going on the meeting).
entries.pattern: [be] going on [number] · [noun phrase] going on [number]
entries.contrast: Nearly and almost are adverbs and go with anything; going on attaches only to numbers, and only from below — you cannot be going on an age you have already passed. The idiom nine going on thirty-five (a knowing child) is a fixed joke built on the same frame.
entries.meaning: Says you are approaching a number — an age, a clock time, or a length of service — without having reached it.
examples: She's going on forty and still won't fly.
It's going on midnight; we should head back.
He's been at the paper going on twenty years.
The kid is six going on thirty.
They've been engaged going on three years now.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ including that he lied). Pronoun objects must be objective: including me, including her and me — ✗ including my wife and I, which is the single most common error made with this word.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], including [noun phrase] · Including [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Postposed counterpart: [noun phrase] included.
entries.contrast: Including opens a partial list; namely and that is introduce a complete one, so including must never be followed by the whole set. Against counting: including works for any set, counting only for tallies. In contracts, including alone can be read as exhaustive, which is why drafters write including but not limited to.
entries.meaning: Names one or more members of a set already mentioned, leaving the rest implied. 1. Naming examples from a larger set. The list is partial by definition. 2. Counting an amount into a total. Usually money, weight, or time.
examples: Several people, including the director, objected.
The package covers five cities, including Nashville.
Everyone was invited, including me.
That's $40, including tax.
The flight takes six hours, including the layover.
All costs, including shipping, are itemized on page two.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or wh-nominal (judging by what he wrote, judging by how fast they settled) — never a finite that-clause (✗ judging by he was late). Judging from takes exactly the same complements.
entries.pattern: Judging by [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Judging from [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause], judging by [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: This is the word the traditionalists recommend in place of fronted based on, and the recommendation is worth understanding: nobody expects a judging to have a subject, so the fronted phrase raises no dangling objection even from readers who dislike Based on the data, we canceled. Against according to, which reports what a source said, judging by draws the speaker's own inference from evidence — according to the reviews quotes them, judging by the reviews reasons from them. Judging by and judging from are freely interchangeable in American English; to judge by and to judge from are the stiffer infinitival variants.
entries.meaning: Marks an inference and its evidence in one stroke, and quietly signals that the speaker could be wrong. 1. Inferring from physical or documentary evidence. 2. Inferring from a report or a manner. Usually with judging from.
examples: Judging by the line outside, the reviews were good.
Judging from her voice, she had been crying.
Judging by what he wrote, he never opened the report.
The house is older than the deed says, judging by the wiring.
Judging by how fast they settled, the evidence was bad.
Judging from two quarters of data, the change is holding.

entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause, and no gerund (✗ lacking having a quorum).
entries.pattern: Lacking [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: Lacking is the living, slightly literary form; wanting is its archaic twin; absent is what an American lawyer writes; failing is used for an act that was not performed rather than a thing that is not there. Keep the preposition apart from the adjective in the report is lacking in detail, which requires in.
entries.meaning: States the absence that forced the outcome. Almost always fronted, and almost always followed by a consequence.
examples: Lacking a quorum, the board adjourned.
Lacking any evidence of intent, prosecutors dropped the charge.
Lacking an heir, he left the farm to the county.
Lacking better options, we took the red-eye.
Lacking federal money, the project stalled for a decade.

entries.type: marginal/participial; also postpositive; also a sentence adverb
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund; in legal drafting only, a finite that-clause (notwithstanding that the parties have agreed). In ordinary prose, keep it to a noun phrase.
entries.pattern: notwithstanding [noun phrase] · [noun phrase] notwithstanding (postposed) · Notwithstanding [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: It means despite, but with three properties despite lacks. First, it can follow its object — the objections notwithstanding — which no other concessive preposition in English can do. Second, it heads the override formula that makes one contract or statute clause defeat another. Third, it can drop its object altogether and stand as a sentence adverb meaning "all the same" (He was warned; he went notwithstanding), where despite is impossible. Despite and in spite of are the everyday words, and all three take a noun phrase or a gerund and never a that-clause outside legal drafting: ✗ despite he was tired, ✗ in spite of that it rained → despite being tired, in spite of the rain. Also ✗ notwithstanding of is an error, exactly like ✗ despite of.
entries.meaning: A calque of Latin non obstante, "not standing in the way," and still the only common English preposition that is equally comfortable before or after its object. 1. Despite (before the object). The ordinary formal use. 2. Despite (after the object). The postpositive use, distinctly literary or legal. 3. The legal override. Notwithstanding any other provision — this clause wins over conflicting ones. 4. Cross-class: the bare adverb. No object at all, meaning "all the same." The preposition takes an object; the adverb does not.
examples: Notwithstanding the delay, the shipment arrived intact.
She took the job notwithstanding the pay cut.
The objections notwithstanding, the vote proceeded.
His reputation notwithstanding, the jury acquitted him.
Notwithstanding any other provision of this Agreement, Section 9 survives termination.
Notwithstanding that the tenant has cured the default, the landlord retains the right of entry.
Notwithstanding having signed the waiver, she sued anyway.
Every engineer on the project objected; the launch went ahead notwithstanding.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause. For a clause use because; owing to the fact that is grammatical but wordy.
entries.pattern: Owing to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] owing to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The traditional rule pairs it against due to: owing to was the adverbial (Owing to fog, the flight was canceled) and due to the adjectival, licensed only after a linking verb (The cancellation was due to fog). American editors have largely abandoned the distinction and fronted due to is now standard, but conservative style guides still flag it — so owing to remains the safe choice in that position. Because of is safer still and sounds like a human wrote it.
entries.meaning: Assigns a cause, at a slightly elevated pitch. Note that bare owing is an adjective meaning unpaid (the balance owing), a different word from this two-word preposition.
examples: Owing to the weather, all flights are grounded.
The museum closed early owing to a power failure.
Owing to an oversight, your invoice was never sent.
Attendance was down, owing to the strike.
Owing to rising costs, the program was scaled back.
Owing to being short-staffed all summer, the branch cut its hours.
The route was closed owing to the bridge having washed out — ✗ owing to that the bridge washed out.

entries.complement: noun phrase naming an event, decision, or process — never a finite clause (✗ pending the board decides → pending the board's decision), and gerunds are awkward (write pending receipt of the report, not pending receiving the report).
entries.pattern: pending [noun phrase] · Pending [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: Until takes a clause and a point in time; pending takes an event as a noun. The by/until rule sits right next to it and is worth having straight: by names a deadline for a single completed action (file it by Friday), until names how long a state goes on (we're closed until Friday), and pending names the event that will end the state rather than the date (we're closed pending the inspection). Awaiting is the near-synonym but keeps a stronger sense of active waiting. Keep the preposition apart from the adjective pending (a pending case, patent pending), which is postposed and means "not yet decided."
entries.meaning: Borrowed from French pendant, "hanging." It suspends the main clause until the named event resolves, and it carries a strong implication that the current state is temporary. 1. Until (an event occurs). The forward-looking sense. 2. While awaiting; during the course of. The overlapping sense, common in legal phrases like pending trial and pending appeal. 3. Cross-class: the adjective. Meaning "not yet decided," used attributively (a pending case) and postpositively (patent pending). It takes no object, which is the whole test — pending the appeal is the preposition, the appeal is pending is the adjective.
examples: The decision is pending review by the board.
She was suspended with pay pending the investigation.
Pending further notice, the office stays closed.
He was held pending trial.
Payments continue pending the outcome of the appeal.
Pending congressional approval, the funds cannot be released.
Two claims are still pending, and the patent is pending as well.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or wh-nominal (pertaining to what was filed) — never a finite that-clause (✗ pertaining to he was hired → pertaining to his hiring). The to is welded on: ✗ pertaining of, ✗ pertaining with, and bare pertaining is not a preposition at all.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] pertaining to [noun phrase] · Pertaining to [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: The heaviest of the topic prepositions. Ranked by weight: plain about is what a person says, regarding is the business default, concerning is a step up, and pertaining to is the top of the scale — it belongs to records requests, statutes, and discovery demands (all documents pertaining to the transaction). Relating to is the same construction one degree lighter and is what most American drafters now write. Against regarding, which merely announces a topic, pertaining to claims that the object belongs to the matter, which is why it survives in law: relevance is exactly what it asserts. Keep it apart from the plain verb pertain, which needs a subject and its own to (the rule pertains to contractors).
variants: relating to (lighter; the current American drafting default)
entries.meaning: Ties a document, a rule, or a record to the matter it belongs to. Its natural home is the filing cabinet, and outside that setting it reads as padding. 1. Belonging to the subject of; relevant to. The legal and archival use. 2. On the topic of. The weakened bureaucratic use, where about would do.
examples: Please produce all records pertaining to the settlement.
The statute pertaining to easements was amended in 1998.
Questions pertaining to benefits go to Human Resources.
Pertaining to your second point, the committee has no view.
She testified only pertaining to what she saw that night.
Documents pertaining to hiring before 2015 were destroyed.
The clause relating to arbitration survives termination.

entries.register: formal; minutes, reports, and legal recitals
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause (✗ preceding she spoke → preceding her remarks, or plain before she spoke). Gerunds are as clumsy here as after following, and a bare measure of time is impossible: ✗ preceding three days → in the three days preceding the vote.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] preceding [noun phrase] · Preceding [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: The mirror image of following, and it inherits every one of following's problems. Before is the plain word, it takes a clause, and it is almost always the better choice; prior to is stiffer still and worse than either. The live trap is cross-class: the far more common attributive adjective in the preceding paragraph and the preceding year modifies the noun it stands in front of and takes no object, while the preposition sits between two noun phrases and relates them (the year preceding the merger). Most readers meet only the adjective, which is why the preposition reads as officialese.
entries.meaning: Places one event immediately in front of another and asserts nothing about cause — which is the one respect in which it is cleaner than following. 1. Immediately before, in sequence. Between two noun phrases. 2. Fronted, opening a clause. The formal adverbial use.
examples: Preceding the vote, the chair read the resolution aloud.
In the week preceding the storm, nobody could buy a generator.
The quarter preceding the recall was the company's best.
Preceding the merger, both firms had already cut staff.
The paragraph preceding this one defines the term.
Preceding that, there had been no complaints at all.

entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard business-correspondence word
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or wh-nominal (regarding what you asked) — never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: regarding [noun phrase] · Regarding [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: The trap is the plural. With regard to is correct; ✗ with regards to is an error — regards belongs only in give my regards. As regards (no to) is also correct but stiff. Among the topic words, regarding is the neutral business default, concerning is heavier, respecting is dated, and plain about or on is usually the best of all.
entries.meaning: Announces the subject of the sentence or the document. In American office writing it has almost entirely displaced concerning.
examples: I'm writing regarding your application.
Regarding the budget, we'll take that up in March.
He had nothing to say regarding the settlement.
Please see the attached memo regarding parking.
Regarding what you asked yesterday, the answer is no.
There are new rules regarding overtime.

entries.register: formal and dated; alive in statutes and constitutional text
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: respecting [noun phrase] · Respecting [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: A synonym of concerning and regarding that has fallen out of ordinary use. It survives chiefly because it appears in famous legal language — Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion — where it means "about," not "showing respect for." That collision with the modern verb respect is the reason to avoid it in new prose.
entries.meaning: The oldest of the surviving topic prepositions. Use it only when you are quoting or deliberately writing in a legal register.
examples: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion.
The treaty is silent respecting fishing rights.
Respecting the second charge, the defense offered no evidence.
Rules respecting the conduct of members were adopted in 1974.
He would say nothing respecting his sources.

entries.register: archaic; survives in legal drafting and set courtesies
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause in modern use. The old conjunction saving that is archaic.
entries.pattern: saving [noun phrase] · Saving [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: The bare preposition save is the surviving literary form (all save one); saving is one step further back. In law it means "without prejudice to," which is why contracts have a savings clause — saving the rights of third parties preserves those rights rather than excluding them. The two readings, "except" and "preserving," are close enough that modern drafters prefer except for or without prejudice to.
entries.meaning: An old except with a legal afterlife.
examples: All the crew survived, saving the second mate.
Saving your presence, ma'am, the man is a fraud.
Nothing was left standing, saving the chimney.
The order is affirmed, saving the appellant's right to seek review.
Every provision remains in force, saving Section 12.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (speaking of getting there early) — never a finite clause (✗ speaking of he is late → speaking of his being late). One extra restriction no other word in this file has: the object must be something already said or obviously in the air. Speaking of cannot introduce a topic out of nowhere, which is why it is a connector and not just a preposition.
entries.pattern: Speaking of [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Speaking of which, [main clause]. — always fronted, always with a comma.
entries.contrast: As for and as to also switch topics, but they are neutral about whether the topic came up before; speaking of insists that it did, and that insistence is the entire meaning of the word. Regarding announces a subject in writing; speaking of picks one up in conversation, and using it in a memo sounds like a transcript. Talking of is the British counterpart and sounds foreign in American speech. The fixed form speaking of which is what you use when the trigger was the whole preceding clause rather than a nameable thing. Do not confuse any of this with generally speaking, strictly speaking, and roughly speaking, which are sentence adverbs, take no object at all, and are not prepositions.
entries.meaning: The pivot of American conversation: it grabs a word someone just said and turns the talk toward it, while pretending the turn was accidental. 1. Picking up a topic just mentioned. With a noun phrase repeated from the previous turn. 2. Speaking of which. With the whole preceding clause as the trigger.
examples: Speaking of the weather, did you hear about the storm Friday?
Speaking of money, we never settled the check.
Speaking of your brother, is he still in Denver?
Speaking of being late, where is Dana?
We need a new roof — speaking of which, the estimate came in.
Speaking of Nashville, that reminds me of the last tour.

entries.register: neutral to informal; the spoken counterpart of beginning
entries.complement: a time expression — a date, a day, a clock time, or a prepositional phrase of time. Never a finite clause, and never an ordinary object in this sense.
entries.pattern: Starting [time], [main clause]. · [main clause] starting [time].
entries.contrast: Starting is what Americans say; beginning is what they print; effective is what the HR notice says; as of is the neutral written form and can also look backward. One redundancy to avoid: starting from Monday — use starting Monday or from Monday on, not both.
entries.meaning: Fixes the first day of a new state of affairs. Purely temporal — it never takes a person or a thing.
examples: Starting Monday, we're on the new schedule.
The pool is open starting Memorial Day.
Starting at nine, calls go straight to voicemail.
Deliveries run twice a week starting in June.
Starting next semester, the class meets online.

entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: touching [noun phrase] · Touching [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: Another dead synonym of concerning. The living modern word spelled the same way is the adjective (a touching tribute) and the verb (touching the wire), so a modern reader hits touching the matter of the will and stumbles. Use concerning or about.
entries.meaning: Survives almost entirely in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century prose and in deliberate pastiche of it.
examples: Touching the matter of the estate, I have written to counsel.
He was examined touching his knowledge of the conspiracy.
Touching these accusations, the bishop was silent.
Nothing in the record is decisive touching the question of intent.
Touching your late letter, I can add little.

entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: Wanting [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [quantity] wanting [quantity].
entries.contrast: Lacking is the modern equivalent for the first sense; minus or less covers the subtractive second sense. Keep the preposition apart from the predicative adjective in he was found wanting and from the ordinary verb want, "desire," which is the meaning most learners assume and which is never right here.
entries.meaning: The older sibling of lacking, from the original sense of want, "to be missing." 1. In the absence of; without. The concessive-causal use. 2. Less; minus. A subtractive use, now confined to old prose and set arithmetic.
examples: Wanting a quorum, the assembly adjourned.
Wanting better evidence, the coroner recorded an open verdict.
Wanting a will, the estate passed to the next of kin.
A hundred wanting three is ninety-seven.
He served forty years wanting two months.
It was a full crew wanting one deckhand.
Wanting any word from headquarters, the captain acted on his own.

entries.register: neutral; standard in American journalism and business writing
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a wh-nominal (based on what he told us) — never a finite that-clause (✗ based on that he told us). For a clause, write because or on the ground that.
entries.pattern: Based on [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [noun phrase] based on [noun phrase]. · [clause], based on [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The famous dangling-modifier fight. Traditionalists object to the sentence-opening use (Based on the data, we canceled the launch) because we are not based on anything, and prescribe on the basis of or judging by instead. American practice has moved: fronted based on is now standard in edited prose. The real participle basing still needs its subject and still dangles (✗ Basing the estimate on last year, the budget was wrong). Against depending on: based on names the evidence behind a settled conclusion, depending on names the variable that has not resolved yet.
entries.meaning: The most contested word in this file, and the clearest case of a participle finishing its journey into a preposition. When it modifies a noun (a film based on a novel) nobody objects; the argument is only about the fronted adverbial. 1. Deriving from a source. Attached to a noun, uncontroversially participial. 2. On the evidence of; according to. The fronted preposition.
examples: The film is based on a novel nobody read.
They built a whole product line based on one patent.
Based on the polling, the race is a toss-up.
Based on what she told me, I'd take the offer.
We rejected the bid based on price alone.
Based on three quarters of data, the trend looks real.
Based on having watched two seasons, I'd say it holds up.

entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ compared to he ran faster → compared to him, compared to his time). The two things compared must be parallel, and this is where the sentence usually breaks: ✗ Her salary is low compared to a manager compares a salary to a person → compared to a manager's or compared with that of a manager. A pronoun object takes the objective case: compared to me, ✗ compared to I.
entries.pattern: [clause], compared to [noun phrase]. · Compared to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [noun phrase] compared with [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The old rule assigned compare to to likening unlike things (shall I compare thee to a summer's day) and compare with to measuring like against like (compare this quarter with last). In the fixed participial preposition the distinction has collapsed in American English, and compared to now covers both; compared with survives as the slightly more formal and more statistical of the two. In comparison with is the heavy version, relative to the technical one. Than is a conjunction and is not an alternative here: ✗ cheaper compared than, either cheaper than or cheap compared to. And versus merely juxtaposes two things, where compared to asserts that a measurement has been made.
variants: compared with (more formal, more common in statistical writing)
entries.meaning: Sets one thing beside another so the difference registers. It is the standard American way to frame a number as good or bad news. 1. Measured against. The quantitative use, the common one. 2. Likened to. The figurative use, where the two things are of different kinds.
examples: Compared to last year, sales are up nine percent.
The rent is cheap compared to Boston.
Compared to the original, the remake is tame.
Enrollment fell four percent, compared with six percent nationally.
Two hours is nothing compared to what that drive used to be.
Compared to being on call every night, this job is a vacation.

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a finite clause with that — given that the deadline had passed. It cannot stand alone as an adverb (✗ She did well, given).
entries.pattern: Given [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Given that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] given [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Against considering: given states a premise and moves on, while considering weighs and often excuses. Against granted: given takes a fact you both accept; granted concedes a point you are about to argue past. Only considering and granted can trail a sentence with no complement at all; given always needs an object. Cross-class, three other words are spelled the same and none of them is this preposition: the plain past participle of give (the money was given anonymously), the attributive adjective meaning "specified" or "prone to" (at any given moment, given to exaggeration), and the count noun (that's a given). The preposition is the one that takes a bare object and modifies the whole clause.
entries.meaning: Treats what follows as established and reasons from it. Its origin is visible in the mathematical use, where the given is literally what you are handed at the start of a proof. 1. In view of; taking as established. The everyday use, with a noun phrase. 2. Given that (with a clause). The same meaning, with a full finite clause — one of only three words in this file that allows one in ordinary prose, alongside considering and granted; the fourth, legal notwithstanding that, is confined to drafting. 3. In mathematics and logic: assumed as a starting condition. 4. Cross-class: the adjective and the noun. A given moment, a given. No object, no clause — and no longer a preposition.
examples: Given the circumstances, the sentence was lenient.
Given his record, the promotion surprised nobody.
Given the shortage of nurses, the wait is no surprise.
Given that she had two days to prepare, the presentation was remarkable.
Given that no one objected, the motion carried.
Given two points, construct the perpendicular bisector.
Given a constant rate of decay, the age can be calculated.
At any given moment, half the fleet is in the shop — and that the schedule slips is now a given.

entries.type: marginal/participial (past participle); also a standalone concessive adverb
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a finite clause with or without that — granted (that) the price is high. It also takes no complement at all as a sentence adverb: Granted, it's expensive.
entries.pattern: Granted [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Granted (that) [clause], [main clause]. · Granted, [main clause].
entries.contrast: Given accepts a premise as neutral fact; granted concedes a point that works against the speaker, and the sentence that follows almost always pushes back — Granted, it's expensive, but.... As a bare adverb it takes a comma and functions like admittedly; given can never do this. The -ing variant granting (that) is slightly more formal and less common.
entries.meaning: The concessive of the pair. It hands the other side a point and then takes the sentence back. 1. Conceding a stated point (with an object or clause). 2. Standing alone as admittedly. No complement, comma after.
examples: Granted the difficulty of the terrain, the survey was fast work.
Granted that the data are thin, the pattern is still suggestive.
Granted, the seats are terrible, but the sound is perfect.
It's a risk, granted, and we're taking it anyway.
Granting his sincerity, the argument still fails.
Granted the premise, the conclusion follows.

entries.ipa: /wɜrθ/ · run together before a weak object: worth it /ˈwɜrθ ɪt/ → /ˈwɜrθət/
entries.type: marginal (traditionally labeled an adjective, but it takes a bare object like a preposition)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause and never a to-infinitive: ✗ worth to see, ✗ worth to be seen → worth seeing. This is one of the most common learner errors in English. The object may be a pronoun: worth it.
entries.pattern: [subject] is worth [noun phrase] · [subject] is worth [verb-ing] · it is worth [verb-ing] · for what it's worth
entries.contrast: Worth takes its object bare; worthy requires of — worth praise but worthy of praise; ✗ worth of praise is the error that comes of mixing them. And the gerund after worth is passive in meaning even though it is active in form: the house is worth fixing up means worth being fixed up, and adding being is wrong (✗ worth being fixed up). Keep the preposition apart from the identical noun, which follows a possessive and takes of: ten dollars' worth of gas, get your money's worth. Note the apostrophe — the measure is possessive, and ten dollars worth is a misspelling.
entries.meaning: The reason worth sits in this file is that it is the one common English word that takes a direct object without being a verb or a preposition by traditional labeling. Every modern grammar that reclassifies it makes it a preposition. 1. Having a stated monetary value. 2. Deserving the time, money, or trouble. Typically with a gerund — and the gerund is where learners reach for the infinitive and go wrong. 3. In fixed phrases. For what it's worth, for all it's worth. 4. Cross-class: the noun. Preceded by a possessive and followed by of, which the preposition never is: a dollar's worth of trouble.
examples: The house is worth about four hundred thousand.
That coin is worth more than the car it came in.
The drive is long, but the view is worth it.
This place is worth visiting twice.
It's worth asking before you assume.
The old boiler is not worth repairing a third time.
For what it's worth, I'd have made the same call.
The agent played up the school district for all it was worth.
We got twenty dollars' worth of gas and our money's worth of advice.

entries.complement: precedes it — a measure-of-time noun phrase (three weeks, a moment, long). It can take nothing after it, ever, and never a clause. The measure phrase is obligatory: ✗ He left ago.
entries.pattern: [measure of time] ago · ✗ ago [measure of time]
entries.contrast: Two rules. First, ago counts back from now and therefore demands the simple past: ✗ He has left three days ago → He left three days ago. Before counts back from a point already in the past: He had left three days before. Second, ago is not interchangeable with for — ago locates an event, for measures a duration (she left three days ago, she was gone for three days). And long since is not a British substitute for long ago, as it is sometimes labeled: it is standard formal American English, and it differs by tense, taking the perfect that ago forbids (the shop has long since closed, ✗ the shop has closed long ago).
entries.meaning: Descended from the past participle of Old English āgān, "to pass by," so it is a participial preposition too — one that finished its journey centuries earlier than the rest of this file and ended up on the wrong side of its object.
examples: Three weeks ago we had no idea.
She called a few minutes ago.
That happened long ago.
The factory closed twenty years ago.
I saw him not five minutes ago.
A century ago, none of this existed.

entries.register: neutral; slightly British in this construction
entries.complement: precedes it — a noun phrase or gerund. Never a clause.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] apart, [main clause].
entries.contrast: Aside is the American default in this frame: joking aside is idiomatic in the U.S., while joking apart reads as British. Do not confuse the postposed apart with the fronted complex preposition apart from, which means "except for" or "in addition to," is itself the British-leaning counterpart of aside from, and lives with the multi-word prepositions. Cross-class, the test is whether anything is being set aside: the postpositive has an object in front of it (cost apart), while the plain adverb has no object at all (the two men drifted apart, I can't tell them apart).
entries.meaning: Sets a topic to one side so the sentence can get to the real point. Almost always fronted as a clause-opening phrase with a comma.
examples: Cost apart, the plan is workable.
Joking apart, we need an answer by noon.
Politics apart, the two men were friends for forty years.
That one incident apart, the trip was flawless.
Style apart, the argument is sound.

entries.register: neutral; the American preference over apart
entries.complement: precedes it — a noun phrase or gerund. Never a clause.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] aside, [main clause].
entries.contrast: Same job as postposed apart, but this is the form Americans use. Note the direction change when it moves to the front: postposed aside only sets something to one side, while fronted aside from can mean either "except for" or "in addition to." Cross-class, the postpositive has an object in front of it (money aside); the ordinary adverb has none (step aside, set it aside), and there is also the theatrical noun an aside.
entries.meaning: Brackets an objection or a topic and moves past it. It is the standard way to signal that you know about the thing you are not going to discuss.
examples: Money aside, the schedule alone kills the project.
Joking aside, that was dangerous.
All modesty aside, I fixed it in ten minutes.
The lighting aside, the room is perfect.
Legal questions aside, is this the right thing to do?

entries.type: complex, built on the postpositive aside
entries.register: neutral; the American counterpart to British-leaning apart from
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a bare finite clause; use aside from the fact that if you must have one.
entries.pattern: Aside from [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] aside from [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The ambiguity is the point of the entry. Aside from has two opposite readings — subtractive ("except for") and additive ("in addition to") — and only the following clause tells you which: Aside from the salary, the job is great subtracts, while Aside from the salary, there are benefits adds. When it matters, write except for for the first and besides or in addition to for the second. Apart from carries exactly the same double reading and is the British preference.
entries.meaning: The most useful and most treacherous member of this group, because both of its meanings are common and neither is marked. 1. Except for. Subtractive: it takes the named thing out of the claim. 2. In addition to. Additive: it puts the named thing alongside what follows.
examples: Aside from the ending, the movie is terrific.
Aside from a sore shoulder, he came through fine.
Aside from the tuition, there are books and fees.
Aside from being late, she brought the wrong file.
Nobody knew, aside from the two of us.
Aside from Nashville, the tour hits four cities in Texas.

entries.complement: precedes it — a measure-of-time noun phrase (a few years, a while). Never a clause, and no object after it.
entries.pattern: [measure of time] back
entries.contrast: It is a casual ago, and it is vaguer — a few years back invites less precision than three years ago. Do not confuse it with the adverbial back in 1998, which comes before its object and is a different construction entirely. Cross-class, the postpositive needs a measure phrase in front of it (a while back), while the ordinary directional adverb needs nothing (come back, she called back), and back is also a common noun and a verb. In writing above the level of a blog post, use ago.
entries.meaning: The conversational alternative to ago, restricted to loose measures of past time.
examples: A few years back, this was all farmland.
I ran into him a while back.
Two summers back, the river came up over the road.
She mentioned it a couple of weeks back.
Some time back, they stopped answering the phone.

entries.register: formal; one fixed phrase is conversational
entries.complement: precedes it — a noun phrase. Never a clause, never anything after it.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] excepted, [main clause]. · [main clause], [noun phrase] excepted.
entries.contrast: The postposed partner of prepositive excepting, and the negative counterpart of postposed included. Against excluded: excepted lifts a person or case out of a general statement, usually as a courtesy or a legal reservation, while excluded removes an item from a price, a set, or a policy. The fixed phrase present company excepted is the one use every American speaker knows.
entries.meaning: Takes someone or something out from under a rule that has just been stated.
examples: Everyone in that office is useless, present company excepted.
All fees are refundable, the application fee excepted.
Sundays excepted, the desk is staffed from eight to six.
The rule binds every member, the treasurer excepted.
Two counties excepted, the state went the other way.

entries.complement: precedes it — a noun phrase. Never a clause.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] excluded, [main clause]. · [main clause], [noun phrase] excluded.
entries.contrast: The mirror of postposed included and the postposed partner of excluding. Against excepted: excluded is arithmetic — it takes an item out of a total or a coverage list — while excepted is a concession about people or cases. On a price tag, tax excluded and excluding tax say the same thing; tax excepted does not exist.
entries.meaning: Removes an item from a price, a set, or a scope of coverage, after the fact.
examples: The rate is $220 a night, taxes excluded.
All finishes are covered, custom colors excluded.
Delivery is free nationwide, Alaska and Hawaii excluded.
Every department gained headcount, contractors excluded.
The warranty covers parts and labor, wear items excluded.

entries.complement: precedes it — a measure-of-time noun phrase (three days, a week, a fortnight). Never a clause, nothing after it.
entries.pattern: [measure of time] hence
entries.contrast: The forward-pointing twin of ago: three days ago looks back, three days hence looks forward. In ordinary American English the phrase is three days from now; hence in this sense is a deliberate literary choice. Keep it apart from the far more common conjunctive adverb hence meaning "therefore," which is the same spelling doing an entirely different job. The test is the measure phrase: the postpositive has one in front of it (two years hence), and the connective adverb has none and instead points back at a whole clause (The road was closed; hence the detour). A third, obsolete sense is spatial and means "from here," surviving only in get thee hence and in henceforth.
entries.meaning: An archaic-flavored survivor. Almost every modern American use of temporal hence is either legal drafting or a bid for gravity. 1. Postpositive: a stated span from now. A measure of time comes first, and nothing follows. 2. Cross-class: the connective adverb. Meaning "therefore," with no measure phrase and no object — not a preposition at all.
examples: The lease expires two years hence.
A century hence, none of these arguments will matter.
The court will reconvene thirty days hence.
What we decide today will be judged a generation hence.
Six months hence, the program will be reviewed.
The bridge was out; hence the four-hour detour.
She had never been told; hence her surprise.

entries.complement: precedes it — a noun phrase. Never a clause. Case matters: myself included and me included are both idiomatic; ✗ I included is not.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] included, [main clause]. · [main clause], [noun phrase] included.
entries.contrast: The postposed partner of including, and it is often the more natural order when the object is a pronoun — everyone, myself included beats everyone, including myself. Its negatives are excluded for items and excepted for people.
entries.meaning: Folds a member back into a set that has just been described, usually with a small note of surprise or self-implication.
examples: Everyone laughed, the judge included.
We all missed it, myself included.
The price is $1,800, shipping included.
Every account was affected, the founders' included.
Four states voted against, ours included.

entries.type: postpositive (traditionally labeled an adjective, but it follows and governs the range in front of it)
entries.complement: precedes it — a stated range, normally two numbers or dates joined by to (1 to 30 inclusive). Never a clause, and nothing may follow it. When something does follow, the word is the prepositive complex preposition inclusive of, which is a different construction (a fee inclusive of tax).
entries.pattern: [start] to [end] inclusive · [range] inclusive
entries.contrast: This is the British repair for exactly the ambiguity American English fixes with through. Monday to Friday inclusive and Monday through Friday name the same five days, but the American form is shorter and is the default in the United States — so an American writes inclusive only in a contract or a specification where nothing may be left to inference. Its opposite postposes the same way: pages 40 to 62 exclusive leaves out page 62. Keep it apart from the ordinary attributive adjective, which stands in front of its noun and means something entirely different (an inclusive definition, an inclusive community); the postpositive has a range in front of it and the attributive has a noun behind it.
entries.meaning: The belt-and-suspenders word. It exists because to does not say whether the last item is in or out, and sometimes that has to be settled on paper.
examples: Sections 4 to 9 inclusive are hereby repealed.
The offer is open December 1 to December 24 inclusive.
Answer questions 1 to 20 inclusive.
Rates apply Monday to Friday inclusive.
The survey covers the years 1990 to 2000 inclusive.
Read chapters 3 to 7 inclusive before the seminar.

entries.type: simple preposition; in the inclusive-range sense a distinctly American connector; postpositive in fixed adverbials; also an adverb, a verb particle, and a predicate adjective
entries.complement: in the range sense, a second date, day, or number, with the first one preceding: Monday through Friday, pages 40 through 62. Never a clause. In the postposed adverbial, the noun phrase comes first: the whole night through. As an adverb and as a particle it takes no object at all — that absence is the test.
entries.pattern: [start] through [end] · [noun phrase] through (postposed adverbial) · [verb] through (adverb or particle, no object) · be through with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: This is the most useful Americanism in the whole file. American Monday through Friday includes Friday. Monday to Friday is ambiguous and British-leaning, and until Friday or till Friday excludes it — I'm here until Friday means you leave on Friday, I'm here through Friday means you leave after it. British writers reach for Monday to Friday inclusive to get the same certainty an American gets from through. Cross-class, the test is the object: the preposition has one (we drove through the tunnel, open Monday through Friday), the adverb does not (we drove through, let me through), the particle binds to the verb and can be separated from it (read it through, see it through, think this through), and the predicate adjective means finished (Are you through?, I'm through with him). The path sense (through the tunnel) belongs with the movement prepositions.
variants: thru (informal American spelling; signage, menus, and drive-thru — never in edited prose)
entries.meaning: Three things qualify it for this file: the inclusive endpoint, which is a genuine grammatical resource American English has and British English does not; the postposed adverbial, a frozen relic in which the object comes first; and the clean cross-class split between the preposition and the object-less adverb. 1. Inclusive range. From the first named point to the second, with the second one counted in. 2. Postposed: for the entire span. Fixed and literary — the whole night through. 3. Cross-class: adverb, particle, predicate adjective. No object anywhere.
examples: The office is open Monday through Friday.
Read pages 40 through 62 for tomorrow.
The exhibit runs June 3 through September 8.
Applications are accepted March through May.
The baby cried the whole night through.
She stayed loyal to him his life through.
The gate was jammed, so we squeezed through.
Read the contract through before you sign it.
Two hours in, I was through with the whole argument.
